name: Peoples of the Great Plains
summary: The peoples of the North American Great Plains, who hunted bison for more than 10,000 years. After horses arrived from Spanish colonies in the 1600s, nations such as the Lakota, Comanche, Cheyenne and Blackfoot became mounted bison hunters.

knownFor.label: Tipi
knownFor.note: A cone-shaped tent of bison hide that could be moved quickly.

knownFor.label: Buffalo jumps
knownFor.note: Herds were driven over cliffs, as at Head-Smashed-In (Alberta), used for about 6,000 years.

knownFor.label: Plains sign language
knownFor.note: Hand signs used to talk between nations with different languages.

location.value: The Great Plains of North America, from Alberta and Saskatchewan to Texas.

terrain.value: Flat or rolling grassland, with river valleys (Missouri, Platte, Arkansas).

climate.value: Continental: hot summers, cold winters, dry winds.

resources.value: Huge herds of bison; river-valley farmland used by some nations.

population.value: Unknown before contact; perhaps a few hundred thousand around 1800.

urbanisation.value: Camps; some nations (Mandan, Pawnee) lived in earth-lodge villages.

disease.value: Smallpox epidemics, such as 1837, devastated the Mandan.

migration.value: Many nations moved onto the Plains from the east and north after getting horses (Lakota, Cheyenne).

economicBase.value: Bison hunting; farming of maize, beans and squash in river valleys.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade networks linking the Plains with the Southwest and the Mississippi; later the fur trade.

governmentType.value: Independent nations with chiefs, councils and warrior societies.

keyRulers.value: Red Cloud, Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse (Lakota); Quanah Parker (Comanche).

succession.value: Chiefs chosen for skill and generosity.

institutions.value: Councils, warrior societies and religious leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Bows, lances; horses from about 1680 and guns from traders.

majorWars.value: Wars between nations; wars with the US Army (Battle of the Little Bighorn, 1876; Wounded Knee, 1890).

territoryChange.value: Lost the Plains to US and Canadian expansion in the late 19th century.

alliancesRivals.value: Alliances such as the Lakota–Cheyenne–Arapaho alliance.

inventions.value: Travois for dragging loads; hide tipis; pemmican (dried meat).

scienceEducation.value: Winter counts: painted calendars of events on hides.

communicationTransport.value: On foot with dogs pulling the travois; from about 1700 horses made travel far faster. Smoke signals and Plains sign language helped across language barriers.

religion.value: Spiritual ceremonies such as the Sun Dance and vision quests.

languageWriting.value: Many languages (Siouan, Algonquian, Uto-Aztecan and others) and Plains sign language.

artsArchitecture.value: Beadwork and quillwork, painted hides, feathered headdresses.

sharedIdentity.value: Separate nations with their own identities.

dailyLife.value: Bison-hide tipis that could be moved quickly, or earth lodges in river villages; bison meat, dried as pemmican; clothes of tanned hide.

neighbours.value: Pueblo peoples, Woodland peoples, Spanish, French, British and Americans.

colonisation.value: Forced onto reservations by the US and Canada; the bison were nearly wiped out (about 1870–1885).

riseSignals.value: The horse transformed Plains life from about 1700.

declineSignals.value: Disease, the destruction of the bison and military conquest.

outcome.value: Plains nations continue today, many on reservations and reserves.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Plains Indians; Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008).

overallCertainty.value: Well documented after contact; earlier history known from archaeology.
